title: Coping with Life Changes
keyIdea: A change is when something in your life is new or different, like a new baby, a new teacher or a new house. Changes happen to everyone. A change can bring lots of feelings at once, like sad and excited, and all of them are OK. It helps to notice what stays the same, to talk to a grown-up you trust, and to use a coping tool, like a favourite toy, slow breaths or a picture plan.

kid: A change is when something is new. A new baby. A new teacher. A new house. Changes happen to everyone.
A change can make you feel lots of things at once. You can be sad and excited at the same time. All your feelings are OK.
Lots of things stay the same. Your bedtime story. Your teddy. Hugs from your family. The same things help you feel safe.
If a change feels hard, tell a grown-up you trust. Take your teddy. Take big, slow breaths. Make a picture plan of the new day.
adult: Starting school, a new teacher, a new baby or moving house are some of the first big changes young children face. In England, primary Health Education asks children to recognise and talk about their emotions. They learn simple self-care and where to get support. The PSHE Association plan for Key Stage 1 covers change and loss, such as moving home or losing a pet, and the feelings they bring. The IB PYP strand on identity also covers coping with change.

Useful words at this age: change (something new or different), routine (what happens the same way each day), feelings, mixed feelings (two feelings at once), trusted adult (a grown-up you know who keeps you safe) and coping tool (something you do that helps a hard feeling get smaller).

Common mistakes: thinking you may only have one feeling, so a child who is excited about a new baby hides the sad or jealous part. Others think a worry should be kept secret, or cope by hiding away or lashing out. Adults slip too, by saying "nothing will change" when it will. Be careful to name the change honestly. Then point to what stays the same: routines, toys and people. Keeping routines steady is one of the best supports.

In the lab your child taps the things that are changes and drags mixed feelings into Mia's heart. They sort what changes and what stays the same at Leo's new school, find trusted people to talk to, and watch a worry meter go down as Mia uses coping tools. Every drag or tap has a big button twin.

familyTip: Before a change, draw a picture plan together: what will be new, and what will stay the same. Name any feelings out loud, even mixed ones ("You can be excited and a bit sad"). Keep bedtime and mealtime routines steady in the weeks around the change.

visual.caption: A change feels hard. Does this help, or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Talk to a grown-up you trust
Hide under the bed all day

lab.caption: Flagship lab: spot changes, fill Mia's heart with mixed feelings, sort what changes and what stays the same, find helpers and shrink a worry with coping tools.

choices: You brush your teeth, like every day
You sleep in your own bed
practice.hint: A change is something new or different.
practice.explain: A new baby is new, so it is a change. Brushing teeth and your own bed stay the same.

practice.prompt: Mia moves house. She has {n} toys. She packs them all, then her teddy too. How many things come with her?
practice.hint: Start with {n} toys and count on 1 more.
practice.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1}. Taking things from home helps a new house feel safe.

practice.prompt: Leo feels sad and excited about his new school. What is true?
choices: You can have two feelings at once
practice.hint: Think about Mia's heart in the lab.
practice.explain: Mixed feelings are normal. Sad and excited can be there together, and both are OK.

practice.prompt: Mia takes {n} big, slow breaths. Then she takes {m} more. How many breaths is that?
practice.hint: Add the {n} breaths and the {m} breaths.
practice.explain: {n} and {m} more is {=n+m} breaths. Slow breaths help a worried body feel calm.

pool.prompt: A change feels hard. Who can you tell?
pool.hint: Pick someone you know who keeps you safe.
pool.explain: A trusted grown-up, like a teacher or someone in your family, can listen and help.

pool.prompt: What helps when a change makes you worried?
pool.hint: Which one makes the worry smaller?
pool.explain: Talking about it helps the worry get smaller. Shouting and hiding keep it big.

pool.prompt: Leo starts a new school. What can stay the same?
pool.explain: At a new school, the classroom and teacher are new. Things at home, like his bedtime story, stay the same.

pool.hint: Grown-ups move house and start new jobs too.
pool.explain: Everyone has changes: children, babies and grown-ups. You are not the only one.

pool.prompt: Which one is a coping tool?
choices: Make a picture plan of the new day
pool.hint: A coping tool helps a hard feeling get smaller.
pool.explain: A picture plan shows what will happen, so there are fewer surprises. That helps.

pool.prompt: A new baby comes home. Sam feels happy and a bit cross. What is true?
pool.hint: Can you have two feelings at once?
pool.explain: Mixed feelings are OK. Sam can tell a grown-up about the cross feeling too.

pool.prompt: Leo had {n} new things on his first day. {s} of them were scary at first. How many were not scary?
pool.hint: Take the {s} scary things away from {n}.
pool.explain: {n} take away {s} is {=n-s}. Lots of new things are fine, and the scary ones get easier.

pool.prompt: Mia has {n} grown-ups she trusts. At her new school, her teacher becomes one too. How many trusted grown-ups now?
pool.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1} trusted grown-ups. More people to talk to helps.

pool.prompt: Which one stays the same when you move house?
pool.hint: Your bedroom and street will be new. What does not change?
pool.explain: Your bedroom and street change, but your family and their love stay the same.
